disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the prediabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is between 5.7% and 6.4%, the range used for prediabetes. This is a common and often reversible stage where lifestyle changes make the biggest difference.

summary: Your HbA1c of 6.4 falls in the prediabetes range, which means your blood sugar is higher than typical but not yet in the diabetes range. Your BMI is in the obese category, and together with low physical activity and fatty liver disease, this adds extra strain on how your body manages blood sugar and fat. The most valuable next steps are keeping up with your HbA1c and liver monitoring, gradually increasing daily movement, and following the food guidance around sugar and alcohol. Small, steady changes now can meaningfully support both your liver health and blood sugar over time.

risk_factors.label: Existing health condition: Fatty liver disease

comorbidity_assessment.note: A liver that stores extra fat can become less responsive to insulin, which may push blood sugar higher over time. Reducing added sugars and working toward a healthier weight can help ease the load on your liver and support better blood sugar balance.

constraints: Cut added sugars and sugary drinks, especially fructose-sweetened ones.

foods_to_eat: Whole grains like brown rice, millets (bajra, jowar) and broken wheat
Pulses and lentils such as moong, chana and rajma
Non-starchy vegetables like spinach, bottle gourd, capsicum and cucumber
Low-fat dairy such as curd and buttermilk in moderate amounts
Nuts and seeds like almonds, walnuts and flax seeds
Fresh whole fruits such as guava, apple and papaya in small portions
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks, packaged juices and sweetened beverages
Sweets, mithai and desserts made with refined sugar
Deep-fried snacks like samosas, pakoras and puris
Refined flour (maida) products such as white bread and bakery items
Processed foods high in added sugar or fructose syrup
plan.portion_guidance: Use a standard katori and bowl as reference: fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with whole grains or millets, and a quarter with pulses or low-fat paneer. Keep oil use to about 1 small spoon per dish and avoid second helpings of grains.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 to 10 glasses of plain water through the day. Buttermilk and herbal teas can be included, but avoid sugary or fructose-sweetened drinks completely.
based_on: fatty liver: emphasis on low added sugar and low fried food
cut added sugars and fructose-sweetened drinks

exercise: Start with 10-15 minutes of brisk walking, 5 days a week, and gradually build up.
Aim to work towards at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming.
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities, like bodyweight exercises (squats, wall push-ups, resistance bands), on 2 days a week.
Break up long periods of sitting with short movement breaks every hour, since your activity level is currently low.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with a 10-minute walk daily this week, then build up to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, over the next 4-6 weeks.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range, and because you also have fatty liver disease, gradually losing 7-10% of your current body weight can meaningfully reduce liver fat and support healthier blood sugar levels over time. Aim for slow, steady progress of about 0.5 to 1 kg per week through a combination of regular physical activity and balanced vegetarian meals, rather than rapid weight loss. Small, sustained changes tend to work best for keeping weight off long-term.
lifestyle.sleep: Try to get 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, even on weekends, avoid screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet to support good rest.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5 minutes a day, especially during stressful moments.
Try a short daily mindfulness or meditation practice using a free app or guided audio.
Consider gentle yoga or stretching, which can help both stress levels and physical activity goals.
Make time for a hobby or social connection each week to support emotional wellbeing.
behaviour_change: Since you drink occasionally, consider keeping alcohol intake minimal or limiting it to special occasions, as alcohol can affect liver health and blood sugar control.
Set small, specific weekly goals (like adding one more walk or one more vegetable-rich meal) rather than trying to change everything at once.
Track your progress with a simple journal or app to notice patterns and celebrate small wins.
Involve family or friends in your walking or meal changes for extra motivation and support.
based_on: Target of 7-10% body weight loss to improve liver fat

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Catches progression from prediabetes to diabetes early.

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Keep track of your HbA1c and fasting blood sugar at the intervals your doctor recommends.
Schedule the liver tests and FIB-4 score check since this was highlighted as a priority.
Add short walks or light activity most days to counter a sedentary routine.
Cut back on added sugars and sugary drinks, especially fructose-sweetened ones, as advised.
Avoid alcohol completely to protect your liver.
Aim for gradual weight loss, since losing even 7–10% of body weight can meaningfully improve liver fat.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
